title: Aesthetics and Psychological Effects of Fractal Based Design
research_question: To examine the aesthetic and perceptual experience of fractal 'global-forest' designs and their local 'tree-seed' components, and to determine how fractal pattern components are associated with positive psychological experiences that can be utilized to promote occupant wellbeing.

participants.description: Experiment 1A: 78 undergraduate Psychology students (66 females, 18-30 years old, mean 20 years old) from University of Oregon, United States. Experiment 1B: 81 undergraduate Psychology students (69 females, 18-47 years old, mean 20.42 years) from UNSW Sydney, Australia. Experiment 2: 39 undergraduate Psychology students (22 females, 18-29 years old, mean 20 years old) from University of Oregon, United States.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Fractal 'global-forest' patterns with D-values of 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, and 1.8 (Experiment 1A & 1B). Each D-value had two arrangements: non-randomized (original forest pattern) and randomized (simulating carpet tile installation). Experiment 1B also included D-values 1.1, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7. Fractal 'tree-seed' patterns with D-values of 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, and 1.8 (Experiment 2).

mechanisms: Fractal patterns ease visual processing, reducing cognitive and visual strain.
Fractal preference is driven by a balance between increased arousal (desire for engagement and complexity) and decreased tension (desire for relaxation or refreshment).
The local 'tree-seed' patterns contribute to the perception of the overall 'global-forest' design.
moderators: participant subgroups (identified via cluster analysis) for preference, refreshment, and relaxation judgments
implementation_implications: Installations of composite mid-high complexity 'global-forest' patterns (D=1.6) can balance contrasting needs for arousal and relaxation, promoting occupant wellbeing.
Fractal designs can be varied in media, location, and artistic style to accommodate changing space requirements and aesthetic elements.
The choice of D-value might depend on occupants and space functionality (e.g., classrooms vs. hospitals).
Non-randomized patterns generally elicit slightly higher positive ratings for engagement, preference, refreshing, and relaxing qualities.

limitations: Participant samples were predominantly from 'WEIRD' (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, limiting generalizability.
The study used self-report measures, which may be subject to bias.
The confirmed fractal scaling range (0.2 to 24 inches) is limited, though expected to continue beyond.
The visibility of tile edges in randomized patterns might be less apparent in real installations than in the experimental stimuli.

paper_metadata.title: Aesthetics and Psychological Effects of Fractal Based Design
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Aesthetics and Psychological Effects of Fractal Based Design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Highly prevalent in nature, fractal patterns possess self-similar components that repeat at varying size scales. The perceptual experience of human-made environments can be impacted with inclusion of these natural patterns. Previous work has demonstrated consistent trends in preference for and complexity estimates of fractal patterns. However, limited information has been gathered on the impact of other visual judgments. Here we examine the aesthetic and perceptual experience of fractal ‘global-forest’ designs already installed in humanmade spaces and demonstrate how fractal pattern components are associated with positive psychological experiences that can be utilized to promote occupant wellbeing. These designs are composite fractal patterns consisting of individual fractal ‘tree-seeds’ which combine to create a ‘global fractal forest.’ The local ‘tree-seed’ patterns, global configuration of tree-seed locations, and overall resulting ‘global-forest’ patterns have fractal qualities. These designs span multiple mediums yet are all intended to lower occupant stress without detracting from the function and overall design of the space. In this series of studies, we first establish divergent relationships between various visual attributes, with pattern complexity, preference, and engagement ratings increasing with fractal complexity compared to ratings of refreshment and relaxation which stay the same or decrease with complexity. Subsequently, we determine that the local constituent fractal (‘tree-seed’) patterns contribute to the perception of the overall fractal design, and address how to balance aesthetic and psychological effects (such as individual experiences of perceived engagement and relaxation) in fractal design installations. This set of studies demonstrates that fractal preference is driven by a balance between increased arousal (desire for engagement and complexity) and decreased tension (desire for relaxation or refreshment). Installations of these composite mid-high complexity ‘global-forest’ patterns consisting of ‘tree-seed’ components balance these contrasting needs, and can serve as a practical implementation of biophilic patterns in human-made environments to promote occupant wellbeing.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Fractal patterns with a dimension (D-value) between 1.3 and 1.5 are perceived as most aesthetically pleasing and have beneficial psychological effects, such as stress reduction.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how the fractal dimension of visual stimuli influences perceived complexity and aesthetic preference, which in turn mediate psychological effects such as stress reduction and restoration.
